design_detail: Essay (European Journal of Epidemiology, section 'Essay'; online-first PDF of 5 pages, 1 figure, 23 references) arguing that Mendelian randomization (MR) is an observational instrumental-variable method that should be renamed genetic instrumental variable analysis (GIVA) and reported without the words randomization or causality. It sets out threats to validity (confounding by population structure and by parental genotype, weak-instrument bias, pleiotropy, adaptation over the life course, inconsistent results), illustrated mainly with two alcohol MR studies (Holmes et al., 2014; Millwood et al., 2019), and contrasts them with the MTHFR and folate example. No search, selection criteria, data or synthesis. Appraised with the editors' narrative-review checklist, as the round brief directs for this essay.
can_establish: Which methodological objections three Harvard nutrition epidemiologists raised in 2019 against Mendelian randomization evidence on alcohol and cardiovascular disease, and which features of two MR studies they offered in support.
cannot_establish: Whether these objections explain the MR findings on alcohol (the essay quantifies none of them and reports no data from the studies it criticizes), what those studies found or how they tested their assumptions (to be taken from the studies themselves), or whether moderate drinking protects the heart.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (essay). The 23 references: the two alcohol MR studies (Holmes et al., 2014; Millwood et al., 2019); population genetics of the ADH genes (Osier et al., 2002); ADH and ALDH polymorphisms and alcohol dependence in four Chinese ethnic groups (Shen et al., 1997); the Adverse Childhood Experiences study (Felitti et al., 1998); a validity study of self-reported drinking (Midanik, 1982); a meta-analysis of interventional studies of alcohol and coronary risk markers (Brien et al., 2011, with Mukamal); the AUDIT-C (Bush et al., 1998); binge drinking among US adults (Naimi et al., 2003); Wood et al. (2018); Roerecke and Rehm (2010) on heavy drinking occasions; a consensus statement on LDL cholesterol (Ference et al., 2017); trends in binge drinking (Grucza et al., 2018); binge drinking in Chinese, Korean and White college students (Luczak et al., 2001); a mouse study of binge drinking and plaque (Liu et al., 2011); a study of binge drinking and vascular function in young adults (Goslawski et al., 2013); three East Asian genetic studies of coronary disease (Takeuchi et al., 2012; Lu et al., 2017; Han et al., 2013); two MTHFR meta-analyses (Klerk et al., 2002; Lewis et al., 2005); a meta-analysis of folic-acid trials for stroke prevention (Hsu et al., 2018); and the VISP trial (Toole et al., 2004).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria; examples chosen by the authors.
sample.selection_effects: The MR evidence on alcohol and cardiovascular disease is represented by two studies, each discussed only for features that support the critique; MR studies published later (Larsson et al., 2020; Biddinger et al., 2022, on the project list) could not be considered; the conventional cohort evidence that the MR studies were designed to test is not discussed.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. The essay notes that self-reported drinking is misclassified in both directions and that drinking has at least three dimensions (frequency, usual quantity, binge drinking), which genetic variants shift together.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable. Outcomes discussed: cardiovascular disease, coronary heart disease, myocardial infarction and stroke, with HDL cholesterol as an intermediate; for folate, homocysteine, coronary heart disease and stroke.
outcomes.operationalization: The validity of MR is judged against the instrumental-variable conditions (an instrument strongly related to the exposure, unconfounded, acting on the outcome only through the exposure), plus adaptation over the life course and replication.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. The essay reports no estimate from any study; its only quantitative content is Fig. 1 (relative Google search interest for terms labelled 'Causality' and 'MR', September 2009 to September 2019) and the statement that Ashkenazi Jews make up about 0.2% of Europe's population.
analysis.selective_reporting: Features of the cited MR studies that support the critique (an association of the variant with education, a null association with HDL cholesterol, stronger associations in drinkers) are described without numbers; features bearing on the same points (the strength of the variant's association with intake, adjustment for ancestry, sensitivity analyses) are not mentioned.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A reasoned list of conditions under which MR estimates for alcohol can be biased (population structure, parental genotype, weak instruments, pleiotropy through acetaldehyde, dimensions of drinking that genes shift together, lifelong rather than adult exposure, inconsistent results), illustrated with qualitative features of two MR studies, and an example (MTHFR and folate) in which genetic findings agreed with randomized trials once folate intake was taken into account.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says that examples like alcohol and cardiovascular disease "demonstrate that it must be treated with all of the circumspection" of observational epidemiology (p. 1); the Summary calls the approach's observational nature incontrovertible and urges dropping randomization and causality from its reports (p. 4). Gaps: (1) the essay shows that these biases are possible, not that they explain the alcohol MR findings: none is quantified, and no estimate, instrument-exposure association or sensitivity analysis from the criticized studies is reported; (2) weak-instrument bias is inferred from a null genotype-HDL association, although the essay itself names the genotype-exposure association as the relevant test and does not report it (the companion card sc_holmes_2014 records a strong association with intake, not checked here); a null association with one intermediate trait bears on that pathway, not on instrument strength; (3) the education association is called clearly likely to reflect ancestry, without data; (4) the alternative readings offered (variants as effect modifiers; MR results as evidence of harm from binge drinking or from drinking in youth) are possibilities, not shown; (5) the biases named for MR (confounding, misclassification, selective publication) apply equally to the conventional cohorts that show a protective association, which the essay does not discuss, so it cannot be read as evidence for protection. The central methodological point, that MR is an observational design whose assumptions must be defended, is sound.

timeline.event: Brien et al.: meta-analysis of interventional studies of alcohol and coronary risk markers, co-authored by Mukamal; the essay's source for alcohol raising HDL cholesterol (ref. 7).
Holmes et al. (BMJ): ADH1B rs1229984 Mendelian randomization analysis, the essay's main example (ref. 1; card sc_holmes_2014, this round).
Wood et al. (Lancet): cited for the different health effects of the dimensions of drinking (ref. 10; card sc_wood_2018, this round).
Millwood et al. (Lancet): China Kadoorie Biobank genetic and conventional analyses, criticized for combining genetic and ecological instruments (ref. 2; card sc_millwood_2019, this round).
This essay: received 20 October, accepted 6 November, published online 24 November 2019; printed in vol. 35 (2020), pp. 93-97, according to the reference record.
Larsson et al. (Circ Genom Precis Med): Mendelian randomization study on the project list, published after this essay and not addressed by it (card sc_larsson_2020, this round).

Biddinger et al. (JAMA Netw Open): UK Biobank Mendelian randomization study; the project list describes this essay as a critique of items 13 to 15, but item 15 (Biddinger) appeared over two years later (card sc_biddinger_2022, this round). No replies or letters are linked in the PDF; none were searched for in this round.

replication.where_it_stands: A methodological critique to be cited, attributed to its authors, for the conditions under which Mendelian randomization estimates for alcohol can be biased. What the MR studies found, and how they tested their assumptions, must be cited from the MR studies themselves (cards this round); the essay does not engage with their numbers. MR studies published after it (Larsson et al., 2020; Biddinger et al., 2022) cannot be judged by it.

funding.funder: Not reported: the PDF has no funding statement ('Acknowledgements: None').
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the online-first PDF.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Nutrition, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (all three authors) and Division of General Medicine Research Section, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (Mukamal). Reference lists read in this round show the authors' earlier work on the protective side of the question: Rimm and Stampfer co-authored a 1996 review and a 1999 meta-analysis whose titles link moderate alcohol to lower coronary risk, and Stampfer a 1995 cohort study of US women, all cited by Di Castelnuovo et al. (2006); Mukamal co-authored the Ronksley et al. (2011) meta-analysis and two cohort studies in the Stockwell et al. (2024) pool, one titled for higher usual intake and lower coronary mortality (Dai et al., 2015). The essay does not mention this work. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the arguments.

what_would_settle_it: Not answerable by an essay. Its objections are testable: Mendelian randomization analyses of alcohol that report instrument strength, use within-family (sibling) designs to remove population structure and parental effects, test the variants in people who never drink, estimate non-linear effects without splitting participants by their reported intake, and separate drinking pattern from volume; and, ultimately, a long-term randomized trial of moderate drinking against abstention with cardiovascular outcomes.

domains.note: No search or criteria; two alcohol MR studies chosen as examples.

The essay is itself a critique of the two MR studies, but it describes selected features without numbers and does not report how those studies addressed the same threats (ancestry adjustment, instrument strength, sensitivity analyses); the evidence for its own counter-arguments (a mouse study, a vascular-function study, the ACE study) is not appraised.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: One of 23 references (Brien et al., 2011) lists an author of the essay; the main examples come from other groups. The authors' wider publication record is noted under funding.

Several alternatives are hedged ('may', 'potentially'), but others are asserted as findings: the education association as clearly likely to reflect ancestry, a stratified result as a perfect example of pleiotropy, the observational nature of MR as incontrovertible.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against the validity of Mendelian randomization estimates for alcohol and cardiovascular disease
domains.note: Only the case against the MR estimates is made; their strengths (a strong, specific instrument; agreement across studies) and the weaknesses of the conventional cohort evidence they were designed to test are not discussed, so the case for the genetic evidence is under-represented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard instrument applies to an essay (METHODS §5.3). Its methodological arguments are coherent and referenced, but the examples are chosen without search, the criticized studies are described selectively and without numbers, and only one side is argued; the overall judgment follows the worst domains. Claims may cite it for the objections it raises to Mendelian randomization studies of alcohol, attributed to its authors; not for what those studies found, and not as evidence that moderate drinking is cardioprotective.

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that Mendelian randomization carries all the limitations of instrumental-variable analysis plus genetic ones (confounding, weak-instrument bias, pleiotropy, adaptation, failure of replication); that it has some use for discrete biochemical pathways such as folate metabolism; that the example of alcohol and cardiovascular disease shows it needs the circumspection due to all observational epidemiology; and that reports should drop randomization and causality and call it genetic instrumental variable analysis (GIVA).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Mukamal_2019_MRCritique.pdf (online-first version, Eur J Epidemiol, published online 24 November 2019; no printed page numbers, pages cited as PDF pages 1 to 5), read in full

key_findings.finding: In the authors' view the only randomization reliably present is which of the parental alleles a person inherits; the assumption that genotype is randomly assigned within a population amounts to assuming randomly assigned parents, so the name implies an unwarranted degree of causal inference.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Mukamal_2019_MRCritique.pdf (online-first version, Eur J Epidemiol, published online 24 November 2019; no printed page numbers, pages cited as PDF pages 1 to 5), read in full

key_findings.finding: The essay states the conditions GIVA requires: no path from genotype to outcome except through the exposure (genotype neither confounded nor acting through other pathways) and a link between loci and exposure strong enough to overcome the variability of the two-step chain.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Mukamal_2019_MRCritique.pdf (online-first version, Eur J Epidemiol, published online 24 November 2019; no printed page numbers, pages cited as PDF pages 1 to 5), read in full

key_findings.finding: Population stratification: the ADH1B rs1229984 variant used in alcohol MR studies is said to be most common in people of East Asian and Middle-Eastern descent, including Jews; in Holmes et al. (ref. 1) it went with lower reported intake but also with more education, which the authors read as reflecting ancestry and a healthier lifestyle. Adjustment with 3 to 5 principal components succeeds only if the subpopulation is large enough to appear among them; Ashkenazi Jews are about 0.2% of Europe's population, and the variant is in linkage disequilibrium with nearby variants.
key_findings.note: No numbers from Holmes et al. are given; the size of the education association is not stated.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Mukamal_2019_MRCritique.pdf (online-first version, Eur J Epidemiol, published online 24 November 2019; no printed page numbers, pages cited as PDF pages 1 to 5), read in full

key_findings.finding: Parental genotype: variants that lower a person's drinking are carried by at least one biological parent; if they lower the risk of alcohol dependence ('alcoholism' in the essay), carriers are less likely to have been raised by a parent with alcoholism, itself cited as a risk factor for later cardiovascular disease (the Adverse Childhood Experiences study).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Mukamal_2019_MRCritique.pdf (online-first version, Eur J Epidemiol, published online 24 November 2019; no printed page numbers, pages cited as PDF pages 1 to 5), read in full

key_findings.finding: Weak instruments: the essay says GIVA should always report the genotype-exposure association, notes that self-reported drinking is misclassified in both directions, and infers likely weak-instrument bias and pleiotropy in Holmes et al. from a null association of genotype with HDL cholesterol, although alcohol raises HDL cholesterol in trials (Brien et al., ref. 7), together with the variant's association with cardiovascular disease.
key_findings.note: The essay does not report the genotype-intake association of Holmes et al.; the companion card sc_holmes_2014 (first reader, not checked here) records 17.2% lower weekly intake in carriers.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Mukamal_2019_MRCritique.pdf (online-first version, Eur J Epidemiol, published online 24 November 2019; no printed page numbers, pages cited as PDF pages 1 to 5), read in full

key_findings.finding: Pleiotropy: the ALDH2 rs671 variant, which influences intake more strongly than ADH1B, acts on many aldehydes and raises acetaldehyde exposure in people who drink, so it may affect risk directly. In Holmes et al., genetic associations were stronger in drinkers than in non-drinkers; the essay says greater toxicity when alcohol is consumed cannot be excluded as the explanation and that such variants can be read as modifying the effect of alcohol rather than only as instruments for it.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Mukamal_2019_MRCritique.pdf (online-first version, Eur J Epidemiol, published online 24 November 2019; no printed page numbers, pages cited as PDF pages 1 to 5), read in full

key_findings.finding: Dimensions of drinking: frequency, usual quantity and binge drinking correlate only partly and differ in their cardiovascular effects (Wood et al., ref. 10); genetic variants lower all three, so GIVA cannot separate them, and MR studies linking intake-lowering variants to lower cardiovascular risk may be showing the harm of binge drinking.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Mukamal_2019_MRCritique.pdf (online-first version, Eur J Epidemiol, published online 24 November 2019; no printed page numbers, pages cited as PDF pages 1 to 5), read in full

key_findings.finding: Adaptation: GIVA tests lifelong (and parental) differences in exposure rather than adult exposure; given heavy drinking patterns in adolescence and early adulthood, their lower prevalence among young adults carrying ALDH2 variants, and the possibility that binge drinking initiates atherosclerosis (a mouse study and a vascular-function study are cited), alcohol MR may be testing youthful binge drinking, with uncertain relevance to limited drinking in mid-life.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Mukamal_2019_MRCritique.pdf (online-first version, Eur J Epidemiol, published online 24 November 2019; no printed page numbers, pages cited as PDF pages 1 to 5), read in full

key_findings.finding: Inconsistency: the China study (Millwood et al., ref. 2), described as combining genetic and ecological instruments, claimed causal, dose-dependent harm for stroke with no effect on myocardial infarction, while three East Asian reports found higher coronary risk with the ALDH2 rs671 variant without claiming a causal benefit of alcohol, which the essay calls the more conservative and appropriate reading.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Mukamal_2019_MRCritique.pdf (online-first version, Eur J Epidemiol, published online 24 November 2019; no printed page numbers, pages cited as PDF pages 1 to 5), read in full

key_findings.finding: Appropriate role: the MTHFR rs1801133 variant is a proxy for methyl-cycle activity, not an instrument for folate intake; its association with cardiovascular disease appears only at low folate intake, which randomized folic-acid trials confirmed for stroke; the authors conclude that without knowledge of folate intake GIVA would not give reliable results (some early reports wrongly concluded the observational associations were refuted), and that this model does not extend easily to alcohol.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Mukamal_2019_MRCritique.pdf (online-first version, Eur J Epidemiol, published online 24 November 2019; no printed page numbers, pages cited as PDF pages 1 to 5), read in full

key_findings.finding: Summary: the authors call the observational nature of the approach incontrovertible and urge the elimination of randomization or causality from its reports, renaming it GIVA.

reporting_issues.issue: The PDF on file is the online-first version (published online 24 November 2019) without volume, issue or page numbers.
reporting_issues.consequence: Anchors cite PDF pages 1 to 5; the printed article is pp. 93-97 of vol. 35 (2020) according to the reference record, which could not be checked against this PDF.

reporting_issues.issue: The essay says GIVA should always report the association of the genetic instrument with the exposure, but when it judges Holmes et al. likely to suffer from weak-instrument bias it reports no genotype-intake association and argues from a null genotype-HDL association instead.
reporting_issues.consequence: The weak-instrument charge cannot be evaluated from the essay; the cited study must be read for the strength of its instrument.

reporting_issues.issue: Fig. 1 (relative changes in searches for the two terms, September 2009 to September 2019) gives only the legend labels 'MR' and 'Causality', with no query strings; the text calls it worldwide interest (Introduction, 2nd paragraph, p. 1). Each series reaches 100 at its own peak (Causality about 2011, MR about 2018; checked on the rendered p. 2), so the two appear to be scaled separately and the figure shows the trend within each term, not their relative levels; if 'MR' was the literal search term, it also captures unrelated uses of the abbreviation.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure cannot show that interest in Mendelian randomization in particular rose, or how it compares with interest in causality.

reporting_issues.issue: The essay calls itself a review ('In this review', Introduction, 4th paragraph; Summary) but describes no review methods.
reporting_issues.consequence: It should not be cited as a review of the MR evidence on alcohol.

reporting_issues.issue: The three East Asian reports offered as inconsistent with Millwood et al. are, by their titles, a genome-wide association study of coronary disease in Japanese people, an exome-chip meta-analysis of lipid and coronary loci, and a meta-analysis of ADH and ALDH2 polymorphisms and coronary disease, not instrumental-variable analyses of alcohol.
reporting_issues.consequence: The inconsistency described is between analyses of different design and purpose, which weakens it as an example of conflicting MR results.

reporting_issues.issue: The parental-confounding argument rests on the premise that variants that lower drinking reduce the risk of alcohol dependence, supported by a single citation (ref. 4, a study of ADH and ALDH polymorphisms among four ethnic groups in China); its bearing on the ADH1B variant in European-descent studies is not shown.
reporting_issues.page: pp. 3 and 5 of the online-first PDF (Confounding, 3rd paragraph; reference 4)
reporting_issues.consequence: Indirect support for one of the essay's arguments; like the others, it is not quantified.
